山崎.note: Japanese colonel, chief of staff of the Third Air Group; Jiang Yongnan's target in Wuchang.

山田弘一.note: The Japanese staff-officer alias Jiang Yongnan uses to reach Yamazaki.

冢田.note: The Eleventh Army commander named in Jiang's cover story.

远藤.note: A Japanese general invoked in Jiang's cover story.

方柄忠.note: The handler who assigns Jiang the Gannan posting and the Wuhan detour.

李青天.note: Commander of the Korean Liberation Army; historical.

三青团.note: The Three People's Principles Youth Corps.

光复军.note: The armed force of the Korean Provisional Government; historical.

三八式.note: The standard Japanese Arisaka bolt-action rifle.

江若水.note: The airfield's English interpreter in Gannan, who turns the Huaqing Pool bathhouse into a smugglers' club; executed. Fictional.

沈近朱.note: The widowed art teacher Jiang Yongnan marries in Liyuan village. Fictional.

淑芬.note: Jiang Ruoshui's wartime wife, a painter of birds and flowers. Fictional.

蒋经国.note: Chiang Kai-shek's son; administered Gannan. Wade-Giles form.

青干班.note: The youth-cadre training course (青年干部训练班) at Liyuan village.

华清池.note: A Ganzhou bathhouse named for the Tang imperial hot springs. Fictional locale.

济州岛.note: The Korean island of Jiang Yongnan's birth.

抗战夫人.note: A de facto second wife taken while separated from one's family by the war.

青年军.note: The Nationalist corps of educated volunteers raised in 1944.

207师.note: A division of the Youth Army, formed 1 January 1945.

军委会.note: The Nationalist supreme military command, chaired by Chiang Kai-shek.

新六军.note: An elite Nationalist army returned from Burma.

太平会.note: A secret fraternity of Christian merchants and officials, presented as legend. Fictional.

韩国临时政府.note: The Korean government-in-exile, based in wartime Chongqing.

委员长.note: The wartime title of Chiang Kai-shek, Chairman of the Military Affairs Commission.

忠勇勋章.en: the Medal of Loyalty and Valor

大司刑.note: The Taiping Society's office for purging its own ranks. Fictional.

嘉陵宾馆.note: The premier hotel of wartime Chongqing.

天灯巷.note: A Chongqing lane, site of Anderson's safe house.

中山陵.note: The tomb of Sun Yat-sen on Purple Mountain, Nanjing.

栖霞寺.note: A great Buddhist monastery northeast of Nanjing.

ch36.note: The Japanese national flag, a red sun-disc on white (the Hinomaru). Chinese wartime slang called it the 膏药旗, the “plaster flag,” because the red disc looked like a round medicinal plaster stuck to a white cloth. Historical.

The Type 38 (三八式) infantry rifle, the standard Arisaka bolt-action rifle of the Japanese army, named for the 38th year of the Meiji era (1905), when it was adopted. It was unusually long, so that with the bayonet fixed it stood taller than the short soldiers who carried it, as the passage notes. Historical.

The Three People’s Principles Youth Corps (三民主义青年团), the Nationalist party’s youth organization, founded in 1938; its cadre training classes drilled young officials and officers. In southern Jiangxi it fell under the reforming administration of Chiang Kai-shek’s son (see the next chapter). Historical.

ch36.anchor: the raid on the Huangshan residence last year, on the thirtieth of August
ch36.note: Chiang Kai-shek kept several official residences in wartime Chongqing; the villa on Huangshan (Mount Huang), east of the city, served as his command retreat. Japanese aircraft raided it in August 1941 while he was chairing a conference of his generals, a near-miss “decapitation” strike. The source dates the raid to 30 August, rendered as printed. Corroborated (the August 1941 raid); the exact day is not independently confirmed here.

ch36.anchor: the Korean Liberation Army, under General Yi Cheong-cheon
ch36.note: The Korean Liberation Army (한국광복군; 光复军, literally the army of “recovered light”) was the military arm of the Korean Provisional Government, founded in Chongqing on 17 September 1940 with Nationalist Chinese backing. Its first commander-in-chief was Ji Cheong-cheon (지청천); the source’s 李青天 renders his adopted surname, and he is also known as Yi Cheong-cheon. Historical (corroborated).

ch36.anchor: two Mausers, one in either hand
ch36.note: The Mauser C96 (驳壳枪, the “box cannon”), a broom-handled semi-automatic pistol often carried in a wooden holster that doubled as a shoulder-stock. Cheap, plentiful, and iconic in the Chinese wars of the era. Historical.

ch37.note: The “Youth-Cadre class” (青干班, short for 青年干部训练班) was a training course for young Nationalist officials and officers, run here under Chiang Ching-kuo’s Gannan administration, the setting of this chapter. Historical.

The phrase is 世外桃源, a “Peach-Blossom Spring beyond the world”: from Tao Yuanming’s fifth-century fable of a fisherman who stumbles on a hidden valley at peace, untouched by the wars outside. It has meant an idyllic refuge ever since. Allusion (corroborated).

The bathhouse borrows the name of the Huaqing Pool (华清池), the imperial hot springs near Xi’an where the Tang emperor Xuanzong bathed with his consort Yang Guifei, a byword for languorous pleasure. The joke is that a smugglers’ bathhouse in reforming, dry Gannan should wear so voluptuous a name. Allusion (historical).

ch37.anchor: he no longer knew where he would sober up, or when
ch37.note: The line echoes a celebrated couplet by the Song lyricist Liu Yong (柳永): “Where shall I sober tonight? A bank of willows, the dawn wind, a waning moon.” It has become shorthand for the drinker’s drifting, solitary melancholy. Allusion (corroborated).

ch37.anchor: Chiang Ching-kuo brought his New Deal to Gannan
ch37.note: Chiang Ching-kuo (蒋经国, 1910–1988), Chiang Kai-shek’s elder son and a future president of Taiwan, administered the Gannan region of southern Jiangxi from 1939 to 1945. His reforming “New Deal” (新政) banned prostitution, opium, and gambling; within a year, the sources agree, the region’s brothels had closed. The conventional Wade–Giles spelling of his name is used. Historical (corroborated).

ch37.anchor: A wartime wife is a wife too
ch37.note: 抗战夫人, a “wartime wife”: the common arrangement by which a man cut off from his family by the fighting took a second, de facto wife where he was posted. The phrase names a whole social phenomenon of the refugee years, half tolerated and half winked at. Cultural (historical).
A proverb, 人走茶凉: “when the man leaves, his tea goes cold” — warmth and attention last only as long as one’s presence or use. Shen Jinzhu turns it on the dead. Idiom.
Doenjang-guk (大酱汤), a Korean stew built on fermented soybean paste, the everyday soup of a Korean household. Jiang, a Korean from Jeju, cooks it as the taste of home. Cultural.

ch37.anchor: Jeju Island, where he was born
ch37.note: Jeju (제주도; 济州岛), the large volcanic island off the southern coast of Korea, is Jiang Yongnan’s birthplace. Geographic.

ch38.note: The Youth Army (青年军) was a corps of educated volunteers raised by the Nationalists in 1944 under the recruiting slogan “a hundred thousand youths, a hundred thousand soldiers.” Its divisions were numbered from 201; the 207th, formed on 1 January 1945, was among the few to see hard fighting. Historical (corroborated).

“The Generalissimo” (委员长, literally the Chairman of the Military Affairs Commission) was the standard wartime title for Chiang Kai-shek, head of the Nationalist government and supreme commander of its armies. Historical.
The Military Affairs Commission (军委会, 军事委员会) was the Nationalist government’s supreme organ of military command throughout the war, chaired by Chiang Kai-shek. Historical.

ch38.anchor: An inch of our rivers and hills for an inch of blood
ch38.note: “An inch of rivers and hills for an inch of blood” (一寸山河一寸血) was half of the couplet coined for the 1944 Youth Army recruiting drive; the other half ran “a hundred thousand youths, a hundred thousand soldiers.” Guo reads it off the medal on Jiang’s chest. Historical (allusion).

The Battle of Mount Song (松山战役), June to September 1944, was the ferocious assault by which the Chinese Expeditionary Force retook the fortified peak of Songshan in western Yunnan and reopened the Burma Road. The dug-in Japanese garrison fought nearly to the last man; Chinese losses ran to some four thousand dead. Historical (corroborated).

Mangyou renders 芒友 (Mong-Yu), the road junction in northern Burma where, in late January 1945, the Chinese Army in India and the Expeditionary Force from Yunnan met and reopened the overland supply route—the Stilwell Road—into China. Historical (corroborated).

A running-key or “book” cipher keys its message to the running text of an agreed book—here an English Hamlet—so that without the same edition (the 母本, the “key text”) the numbers cannot be read back into words. Yang Qun has had to reconstruct both the book and the English-to-Chinese step. Technical.

The Taiping Society (太平会) is offered here as rumor: a shadowy fraternity of Christian merchants and officials said to reach into every ministry. No such organization is historically attested; it is the novel’s own invention, and unrelated to the nineteenth-century Taiping Rebellion. Fictional (presented as legend).

ch39.note: The phrase is 连坐, the old principle of collective liability by which a criminal’s kin or associates were punished along with him—a recurring instrument of Chinese statecraft from the Qin dynasty onward. Jiang’s captors hold his brother’s family, still inside China, hostage against his silence. Historical (the legal principle).

Old Jin’s phrase is 摆龙门阵 (bǎi lóngménzhèn), Sichuanese for idle storytelling or shooting the breeze, literally “laying out the Dragon-Gate array.” It marks him, like his oaths, as a Sichuan man. Idiom (dialect).

除夕, the eve of the lunar New Year and the last day of the year, is the great family reunion of the Chinese calendar, kept with fireworks and red lanterns. The lanterns and fireworks of these closing scenes set Jiang’s execution and Tang Ya’s revenge against the most domestic of festivals. Cultural.

ch40.anchor: a grand return-to-the-capital ceremony at the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing
ch40.note: With Japan defeated, the Nationalist government moved its capital back from wartime Chongqing to Nanjing; the return (还都) was proclaimed on 5 May 1946. The Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum (中山陵), the monumental tomb of the republic’s founder on Purple Mountain east of Nanjing, was the natural site for such state ritual. Historical (corroborated: the return was declared 5 May 1946).

Qixia Temple (栖霞寺), on Qixia Mountain northeast of Nanjing, is one of the great Buddhist monasteries of the south, founded in the fifth century and famed for the Thousand-Buddha carvings on its cliff; during the 1937 massacre it sheltered thousands of refugees. Guo keeps his fast here on the very day of the capital’s triumphant return. Historical.
A 沙弥 (Sanskrit śrāmaṇera) is a novice monk, a boy or young man who has taken the preliminary vows but not yet full ordination. Historical (Buddhist).

The Chinese for a shot glass is 子弹杯, literally a “bullet cup.” The closing scene turns the idiom over quietly, given the cyanide coin, the sniper’s bullet, and the drink that shares the poison’s name. Wordplay lost in translation.
